title: A scalable actuarial architecture for financing correlated catastrophes

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a repeatable way to arrange financial protection against catastrophes that damage many policyholders at once. It would connect transparent descriptions of exposed assets and potential losses with committed capital, clear payout rules and disclosed arrangements for financing subsequent events. Its purpose is to make dependable catastrophe financing easier to establish and extend across regions and participants. This is a proposed improvement over existing mechanisms; the supplied evidence does not establish that the entire capability is absent today.

The underlying difficulty is that adding policies exposed to the same catastrophe provides limited diversification. A sufficiently widespread event can generate claims that exceed available risk-bearing capacity. Existing catastrophe bonds and sovereign risk-transfer arrangements already address parts of this problem by assigning specified risks to insurers or investors. They also face modeling requirements, transaction costs and contractual complexity, while systemic cyber risks illustrate how dependence between losses can constrain insurability.

As a synthesis of the proposed design, its actuarial core would estimate how losses occur together, price the protection, assess capital adequacy and allocate losses across events and financing layers. Each layer would identify who pays, under what conditions and up to what limit. Delivery would also require insurance law, structured finance, public finance and market infrastructure. The proposed novelty lies in demonstrably better access, reliability, replication and total friction across these functions.

significance.text: If successful, the architecture could make larger amounts of prearranged, loss-absorbing capital available when a catastrophe overwhelms local pooling. The direct benefit would be more dependable transfer of a financial shock before it occurs. The World Bank’s catastrophe-bond mechanism illustrates the causal basis: a triggering disaster can reduce investor principal to fund the client’s payout. The revolutionary step would be a large, reproducible improvement in access and dependable capacity beyond what existing arrangements already provide.

Conditional downstream possibilities include extending useful protection to smaller pools and enabling more households, firms and governments to arrange financing before disaster strikes. These extensions would depend on suitable distribution, enforceable contracts, affordable administration and willing capital providers. The sovereign transactions in the supplied evidence do not by themselves demonstrate access for households or firms. Whether the advance deserves revolutionary significance would depend on the magnitude and reproducibility of its improvement over comparable existing programs.

Financial risk transfer does not eliminate the underlying catastrophe loss or necessarily reduce physical damage. Someone must ultimately absorb the cost through invested capital, retained losses, future contributions or public financing. Nor does broader participation automatically make strongly correlated risks diversifiable or premiums affordable. The cyber-insurance review’s finding that capital-market participation remains limited and largely untested for systemic cyber events is an important boundary on extrapolating from established catastrophe-financing mechanisms.

missing_breakthrough.text: The unresolved capability is a demonstrably scalable combination of credible loss estimates, committed financing, understandable payout contracts and workable replenishment after severe losses. Existing instruments already combine some of these elements. What remains to be established for this candidate is whether an integrated architecture can deliver materially broader protection and lower total friction while maintaining dependable loss-bearing capacity across correlated events and different participants.

A central scientific barrier is estimating the joint distribution of losses: which exposures fail together, how severe their combined losses can become and how uncertain those estimates are. The supplied cyber-insurance material identifies accumulation risk, pricing difficulties and systemic events whose costs may exceed insurers’ capacity. Severe-scenario tests can inform solvency assessment, underwriting limits, pricing and reinsurance, but their conclusions remain dependent on the scenarios and assumptions used. Modeling cannot turn an inadequately financed exposure into a reliably financed one.

The engineering and institutional barriers include reducing modeling and transaction costs, making contractual coverage clear, securing credible commitments for each loss layer and specifying financing beyond the first event. The World Bank note reports that catastrophe bonds involve greater complexity, modeling requirements and transaction costs than traditional reinsurance; the cyber review documents coverage ambiguity and capacity limitations. Proposed design work must also address basis risk—the possibility that the contractual payout differs from the actual loss—and disclose who bears losses beyond the program’s limits. The supplied evidence does not establish a general pattern of capital withdrawal after losses, so that assertion is not treated as a demonstrated barrier.

current_state.text: Catastrophe bonds and sovereign disaster-risk transfer are established mechanisms. The World Bank’s Disaster Risk Transfer product note, updated as of May 2026, reports 56 transactions providing approximately $6.7 billion of coverage to countries for earthquake, hurricane, tsunami, drought and pandemic events. This includes 32 catastrophe bonds totaling $4.9 billion. These are cumulative coverage and transaction figures, not reported claims payments or proof of the proposed architecture’s superiority. The note also describes investors bearing the risk of losing some or all of their invested capital when a triggering disaster occurs.

Adrien Currat, Joe Perry and Jeffery Yong’s Cyber insurance unpacked: the corporate digital safety net, published as FSI Insights No 75 on 17 June 2026, describes increasingly systemic interconnected cyber incidents. Its overview identifies limited coverage and continuing difficulties with coverage ambiguity, pricing and accumulation risk. Available passages explain that some systemic risks are difficult to diversify and could exceed insurers’ risk-bearing capacity. Capital-market participation is described as limited and largely untested for systemic cyber events. These findings document both existing activity and remaining constraints; they do not demonstrate that the proposed architecture can finance all such losses.

The supplied review assessed the World Bank note’s complete three-page text; figures were not inspected and were unnecessary for the reported findings. Its assessment of the BIS publication relied on a partial landing-page view and a paper extraction that truncates on PDF page 30. The passages supporting the findings above occur before that truncation. These access limits constrain conclusions about the unreviewed material without negating the available evidence.

The supplied record establishes these dated mechanisms and findings, but contains no demonstration of the proposed radical improvement in access, scale or replication. It also contains no bounded freshness-search results establishing subsequent developments beyond the May and June 2026 documents. An earlier October 2024 World Bank snapshot was not supplied, so the assertion that the May 2026 copy replaced that particular snapshot cannot be verified. These are limits on the available record, not evidence that later developments or comparable architectures do not exist.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration: establish independently audited programs in multiple regions covering materially correlated catastrophe scenarios, with named parties contractually committed to each loss layer. Before evaluation, specify covered exposures, event combinations, payout triggers, payment deadlines, financing limits and comparison arrangements. Define measurable thresholds for materially broader coverage and lower total friction, including modeling, transaction and administration costs. These would be proposed evaluation criteria, not established industry standards.
completion_criteria.label: Audited multiregion programs demonstrate broader coverage and lower total friction

completion_criteria.text: Proposed operational and resilience evidence: demonstrate prompt payments in actual operation, then subject capital adequacy to independently challenged stress tests involving specified simultaneous severe losses and successive events. Show how capital would be replenished on disclosed terms and distinguish binding commitments from assumptions about future fundraising. The rationale for stress testing is supported by the cyber review’s discussion of solvency resilience, underwriting and reinsurance; the particular audit, replenishment and acceptance requirements here are proposals.
completion_criteria.label: Prompt operational payments and stressed capital adequacy with disclosed replenishment

completion_criteria.text: Proposed reproducibility and disclosure requirements: reproduce the improvement across independently administered programs, regions and relevant exposure types, comparing arrangements with sufficiently similar coverage and risk. Disclose subsidies, public guarantees, retained losses, basis risk, model uncertainty and the ultimate bearers of extreme losses. Report whether favorable results depend on unusually strong sponsors or favorable financing conditions. More coverage supported by undisclosed guarantees would not establish that the architecture itself had reduced financing friction.
completion_criteria.label: Independent programs reproduce improvements across regions with full financial disclosures

completion_criteria.text: Proposed interpretation boundary: successful tests and operating programs would establish demonstrated breadth within their specified scenarios, contracts and financing conditions. They would not establish literal universality, survival outside the tested assumptions or coverage for every imaginable catastrophe. Practical completion would require explicit limits on covered losses, payout timing and available capital so users can understand what protection has actually been demonstrated.
completion_criteria.label: Explicit coverage, payout timing and capital limits bound demonstrated protection

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis: ACT-01, Reliable actuarial measurement of unprecedented catastrophe losses, addresses the loss estimates and uncertainty needed to price coverage and size capital. ACT-03 uses such estimates to organize financing and allocate losses. Better measurement would strengthen the architecture, but would not itself secure investors, establish enforceable obligations or provide sufficient capital.

Roster-based synthesis: ACT-02, Trustworthy, near-instant insurance settlement at negligible per-claim cost, overlaps with the administration and payout side of ACT-03. Faster, cheaper settlement could reduce friction and improve the usefulness of catastrophe protection. Settlement capability and financing capacity remain distinct: a reliable payment process still requires money available under the relevant contract.

Roster-based synthesis: ACT-04, Reliable long-horizon mortality and longevity forecasting with honest uncertainty, and ACT-06, Reliable long-term actuarial projection of healthcare costs under structural change, concern estimating particular long-term liabilities. Their projections could inform financing when a program includes relevant exposures, but neither forecasting capability establishes an architecture for funding correlated catastrophes. ACT-03 concerns who commits capital and absorbs losses; ACT-04 and ACT-06 concern what obligations may arise and how uncertain they are.

Roster-based synthesis: ACT-05, Dependable long-horizon economic scenarios for actuarial liabilities, overlaps with assessing investment returns, capital availability and financing conditions over time. Such scenarios could inform ACT-03’s stress tests and replenishment assumptions. Economic scenario generation and contractual catastrophe financing remain separate capabilities, and neither guarantees the other’s reliability.

Roster-based synthesis: ACT-07, Accessible lifetime retirement income through transparent, resilient risk pooling, shares concerns about transparent obligations, capital resilience and allocation of losses among participants. Its objective is lifetime retirement income, whereas ACT-03 addresses financing correlated catastrophe shocks. Techniques for pooling and disclosure may transfer between them, but success in either setting would not establish success in the other.

unresolved_issues: Whether a comparable integrated architecture already exists, and which specific improvements would establish ACT-03’s novelty, remain unestablished.
The supplied material does not quantify achievable reductions in total friction, increases in coverage or benefits for smaller pools, households and firms.
The demonstration’s regions, exposure types, event combinations, payment deadlines, comparison programs and acceptance thresholds remain to be specified.
The feasibility and cost of committed capital replenishment after simultaneous or successive severe losses remain to be demonstrated.
The earlier October 2024 World Bank artifact is absent, so its relationship to the supplied May 2026 copy cannot be verified.
Developments beyond the supplied May and June 2026 documents remain unassessed because no bounded freshness-search results were provided.

The BIS paper extraction truncates on PDF page 30. The source index also lists a summary PDF, but the supplied review provides no findings from it; no additional conclusions are drawn from that artifact.

brief.title: Dependable disaster funding across regions
possible: Households, businesses and governments could arrange more dependable financial protection before a disaster strikes, including when many suffer losses together. A repeatable system would link estimates of potential losses to committed money, clear payment rules and plans for financing later disasters.
why: When a catastrophe hits many policyholders at once, local insurance funds can be overwhelmed. Bringing in money committed by outside investors and insurers could make larger amounts available to absorb the financial shock.
Making these arrangements easier to repeat and cheaper to administer could extend useful protection to smaller groups and more regions.

sources.showed: The World Bank has arranged disaster protection for countries through insurers and catastrophe bonds, investments whose money can fund disaster payouts. Payments depend on specified event conditions rather than measured losses.
sources.quote:
WB DRT transactions have all been parametric with 
payouts triggered by the physical parameters of an 
event rather than actual losses incurred.
sources.cited_for: Existing arrangements already connect disaster protection to insurers and investors, with added costs and complexity.
sources.not_established: These transactions do not establish a repeatable system with materially broader protection and lower overall costs.

sources.who: Adrien Currat, Joe Perry and Jeffery Yong
sources.showed: Their review found that cyber insurance leaves substantial losses uncovered. Shared dependence on software and infrastructure can cause losses across many policies, while unclear contracts and difficult pricing constrain protection.
sources.quote:
It is estimated that only 1% of global economic 
cyber losses are covered  by cyber insurance , with small and medium -sized enterprises (SMEs) being the 
most underinsured commercial customers.
sources.cited_for: Disasters that cause many losses together can exceed insurers’ financial capacity and are difficult to price.
sources.not_established: The review does not demonstrate dependable financing for widespread cyber losses; investor participation remains largely untested for such events.

shown: The World Bank has arranged approximately $6.7 billion in disaster coverage for countries. Its catastrophe bonds put investors’ money at risk to fund payouts when agreed disaster conditions occur. This establishes a working mechanism for moving financial risk beyond the affected country.
missing: An integrated system has yet to demonstrate materially broader protection at lower overall cost than comparable existing arrangements.
Dependable financing through simultaneous and successive disasters, including committed replacement funding, remains to be demonstrated.
Credible estimates of losses occurring together, clear contracts and disclosed responsibility for losses beyond funding limits must work together.

milestones.label: Audited regional programs deliver broader protection with lower costs
milestones.explanation: Independent audits would have to show broader coverage and lower overall costs across regions, against preset comparisons, with committed payers for each share of losses. This would establish a measurable improvement.

milestones.label: Prompt payments and resilient funding through repeated disasters
milestones.explanation: Operating programs would have to pay promptly, withstand independently challenged tests of simultaneous and successive disasters, and disclose committed replacement funding. This would test protection beyond the initial event.

milestones.label: Independent programs repeat gains with full financial disclosure
milestones.explanation: Independent programs would have to repeat gains across regions and risks, comparing similar protection and disclosing subsidies, guarantees, uncertainties and who bears losses. This would test whether the gains depend on special support.

milestones.label: Demonstrated protection has explicit coverage, payment and funding limits
milestones.explanation: Successful programs would have to state covered losses, payment timing and available funds within tested conditions. This would let users understand the demonstrated protection and its boundaries.

uncertain: Whether a comparable integrated system already exists, and what improvement would distinguish this approach, remains unresolved.
The size of achievable cost reductions and benefits for households, businesses and smaller groups is unknown.
The regions, disaster combinations, payment deadlines and thresholds for judging success remain to be defined.

page.title: Layered catastrophe risk financing
page.definition: A system assigns different ranges of catastrophe loss to reserves, insurers and investors, with money committed before events and contractual financing for later events. Independently operated programmes demonstrate broader protection at lower cost for comparable covered risk.

goal.need: By May 2026, the World Bank had arranged 56 disaster-risk-transfer transactions providing approximately US$6.7 billion of cumulative coverage. Gaps remain for correlated risks: a Financial Stability Institute review published on 17 June 2026 estimates that cyber insurance covers only 1% of global economic cyber losses and describes capital-market participation as largely untested for systemic cyber events.

statements.quote: Developing an ex ante plan or plans, as necessary, to ensure adequate funding to address the impacts of disasters on public finances
statements.context: Section IV.2 of the recommendation revised on 8 November 2023 addresses public funding, borrowing and risk transfer together.

statements.body: Global Shield against Climate Risks, a G7–V20 initiative
statements.quote: Scale up pre-arranged finance through a global, flexible, and collaborative financing structure.
statements.context: The third high-level goal in Global Shield Ambition.

statements.quote: The proportion of publicly supported macro-level schemes meeting the relevant benchmarks will increase by 10 percentage points.
statements.context: The cost-effectiveness result area of Vision 2025; this is a programme target, not certification of a financing architecture.

completion.title: Independent programmes extend catastrophe protection at lower cost through successive events.
completion.criterion: At least two independently operated programmes in different regions implement the same financing design. Each extends protection to additional exposed participants at lower total cost per dollar of expected covered loss than a matched existing arrangement, without weakening payout terms. Contracts specify loss layers, triggers, payment deadlines, limits and financing for a subsequent covered event; each programme fulfils those commitments through successive events. Cost comparisons include modelling, issuance, administration and financing, with subsidies, guarantees, retained losses and model uncertainty accounted for. This is a provisional Atlas test.
completion.basis: Searched OECD disaster-finance guidance, InsuResilience Vision 2025 and its evaluation framework, Global Shield Ambition, World Bank transaction procedures and CCRIF operating criteria. They supply goals and component tests, but no integrated acceptance test for replication, comparative total cost and financing after losses. The provisional test combines their access, cost-effectiveness and pre-arrangement goals.

milestones.title: A hurricane-loss model passes every Florida Commission acceptance standard.
milestones.criterion: A model receives Florida Commission acceptance under every standard applicable to its submission, following technical review and Commission voting. The quoted requirement is from the 2025 process. Under the earlier 2023 standards, Florida International University's Florida Public Hurricane Loss Model Version 8.3 was accepted on 13 June 2025. Acceptance concerns residential hurricane insurance pricing in Florida.
milestones.set_by: Florida Commission on Hurricane Loss Projection Methodology, Hurricane Standards Report of Activities, acceptability process; this criterion is specific to Florida residential hurricane-loss models.
milestones.threshold_quote: To be determined acceptable, the model shall have been found acceptable for all standards.

milestones.title: A catastrophe bond commits investor principal to fund contracted disaster payouts.
milestones.criterion: A client signs a risk-transfer agreement specifying payout conditions, and the World Bank simultaneously issues a catastrophe bond transferring that risk to investors. A triggering event reduces bond principal by the client's payout. By May 2026, the Bank reported 32 catastrophe bonds totalling US$4.9 billion of cumulative coverage; this is not a measure of outstanding capital.
milestones.set_by: World Bank Treasury, Disaster Risk Transfer product note, published catastrophe-bond transaction procedure.
milestones.threshold_quote: Simultaneously, the WB issues a cat bond, transferring the client’s disaster risk to investors.

milestones.title: A catastrophe pool meets CCRIF's 1-in-1,000 annual claims-paying standard.
milestones.criterion: Modelled resources suffice to pay contractual claims from an event sequence at the 1-in-1,000 annual survivability level specified in CCRIF's Operations Manual. Resources include capital and reinsurance. CCRIF's undated FAQ reports capacity beyond that level and specifies proportional payment if annual claims exceed available resources. This is an operator-reported modelling result, not observed survival of a 1-in-1,000 event sequence.
milestones.set_by: CCRIF, Operations Manual survivability level as published in its RTFS FAQs; a criterion for its regional sovereign risk pool.
milestones.threshold_quote: While 1 in 1,000 is the survivability level that is incorporated into CCRIF’s Operations Manual

milestones.title: A catastrophe insurer pays a triggered sovereign claim within 14 days of the event.
milestones.criterion: The insurer transfers the contractual payout to the insured government within 14 days of the covered event. CCRIF reported paying Guatemala US$6,376,184 on 1 July 2024 following the rainfall event spanning 13 June to 19 June 2024. This is one sovereign policy payout reported in an operator press release, not peer reviewed; it does not measure delivery to households.
milestones.set_by: CCRIF, published 14-day payout commitment for its parametric insurance, which pays against predefined event conditions.
milestones.threshold_quote: CCRIF’s payouts within 14 days of an event

milestones.title: A catastrophe policy regains its full coverage limit after a payout exhausts it.
milestones.criterion: A purchased reinstatement endorsement restores an exhausted policy's full limit during the same policy year. CCRIF reported immediately reinstating Guatemala's excess-rainfall cover to US$6.38 million after its full-limit payout on 1 July 2024. The restored cover ended upon another exhaustion or on 31 May 2025. This one-policy result is from an operator press release, not peer reviewed.
milestones.set_by: CCRIF, Reinstatement of Sum Insured Cover endorsement; the reported demonstration concerns sovereign excess-rainfall insurance.
milestones.threshold_quote: policy to be reinstated if it reaches the coverage limit before the end of the policy year.

milestones.title: A sovereign catastrophe-insurance scheme's annual expenses fall below 20% of premiums.
milestones.criterion: A publicly supported sovereign catastrophe-insurance scheme has annual reinsurance and other expenses below 20% of premiums, using InsuResilience's preliminary benchmark. This measures expenses, not total financing cost or solvency. A 2024 review reported that 24% of macro-level projects self-reported meeting relevant benchmarks in 2022. Interviews with 8 of 15 sampled macro-level schemes could not verify compliance because detailed cost breakdowns were unavailable.
milestones.set_by: InsuResilience Global Partnership, Vision 2025 Background Note, Table 2; the preliminary numerical benchmark for publicly supported sovereign insurance is stated in a table.

not_found: No independent cross-programme study was found establishing broader protection, lower costs for comparable covered risk and fulfilled subsequent-event financing together.

results.finding: The World Bank reported 32 catastrophe bonds providing $4.9 billion in cumulative coverage.
results.detail: Clients sign risk-transfer agreements with pre-agreed payout criteria while the Bank issues bonds to investors. A triggering disaster reduces bond principal by the amount of the client's payout. The coverage total is cumulative, not outstanding capital.
results.quote: This includes 32 cat bonds, totaling $4.9 billion.

results.finding: FIU Florida Public Hurricane Loss Model Version 8.3: 1 model accepted under the 2023 Hurricane Standards.
results.detail: The Commission reports its review and acceptance on June 13, 2025. The summary does not describe the vote and states that the official minutes are the recorded transcript.
results.quote:
The Commission found the FIU Florida Public Hurricane Loss Model Version 8.3 acceptable 
under the 2023 Hurricane Standards.

results.finding: Jamaica’s 2024 catastrophe bond, placed with 15 investors, paid $150 million after Hurricane Melissa.
results.detail: The World Bank simultaneously issued the bond and entered a risk-transfer agreement with Jamaica. The parametric trigger specified payout rates of up to 100% of principal; the bond was fully redeemed after the payout.
results.quote:
Category 5 hurricane Melissa hit Jamaica on 
October 28, 2025, triggering a full payout of $150 
million. Jamaica received the funds on December 1, 
2025 and the bond was fully redeemed.

results.finding: CCRIF made 25 payouts to member countries, all within 14 days of eligible events.
results.detail: The World Bank project report describes the payouts as consistent with policy terms. It does not provide event and transfer dates for each payout.
results.quote:
During the life of the project 
(July 2021–November 2024), 25 payouts were made for a total of US$218.5 million, primarily under the tropical 
cyclone coverage (61 percent), all within 14 days of the eligible event.
